summary.text: Take \(k=31\) and \(s=1\): the divisor sums for \(n=5\) and \(n=1829=31\cdot59\) are respectively \(1/32+1/36\) and \(1/32+1/62+1/90+1/1860\). Since \(1/62+1/90+1/1860=1/36\), both sums equal \(17/288\), so distinct positive inputs have the same fractional part.

full_proof.text:
For positive integers \(n,k,s\), write
\[
F_{k,s}(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}\frac{1}{(d+k)^s}.
\]
The conjecture says, in particular, that for every pair of positive integers \(k,s\), the fractional parts of the numbers \(F_{k,s}(n)\), as \(n\) ranges over the positive integers, are pairwise distinct. Equivalently, for fixed positive \(k,s\), if \(n_1,n_2>0\) and
\[
\operatorname{frac}(F_{k,s}(n_1))=
\operatorname{frac}(F_{k,s}(n_2)),
\]
then \(n_1=n_2\). We disprove this injectivity assertion by giving two distinct positive indices for which the sums themselves are equal.

Take
\[
k=31,\qquad s=1,
\]
and consider \(n_1=5\) and \(n_2=1829\).

First determine their positive divisors. Since \(5\) is prime, its positive divisors are exactly
\[
1,5.
\]
Consequently,
\[
F_{31,1}(5)
 =\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{5+31}
 =\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}.
\]
Putting these two fractions over the common denominator \(288\) gives
\[
F_{31,1}(5)
 =\frac9{288}+\frac8{288}
 =\frac{17}{288}.
\]

Next observe that
\[
1829=31\cdot 59.
\]
Both factors are prime. Indeed, to check that \(31\) is prime it is enough to test the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{31}<6\), namely \(2,3,5\), none of which divides \(31\). Similarly, the primes not exceeding \(\sqrt{59}<8\) are \(2,3,5,7\), and none divides \(59\). The two primes are distinct, so the positive divisors of \(1829=31\cdot59\) are exactly
\[
1,31,59,1829.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_{31,1}(1829)
 &=\frac1{1+31}+\frac1{31+31}
   +\frac1{59+31}+\frac1{1829+31}\\
 &=\frac1{32}+\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The last three terms combine to \(1/36\). To see this directly, use the common denominator \(5580\):
\[
\frac1{62}+\frac1{90}+\frac1{1860}
 =\frac{90}{5580}+\frac{62}{5580}+\frac3{5580}
 =\frac{155}{5580}.
\]
Since \(5580=155\cdot36\), this is
\[
\frac{155}{5580}=\frac1{36}.
\]
Therefore
\[
F_{31,1}(1829)
 =\frac1{32}+\frac1{36}
 =\frac{17}{288}.
\]
Thus we have the exact equality
\[
F_{31,1}(5)=F_{31,1}(1829)=\frac{17}{288}.
\]
Equal rational numbers necessarily have equal fractional parts, so
\[
\operatorname{frac}(F_{31,1}(5))
 =\operatorname{frac}(F_{31,1}(1829)).
\]
However, \(5\ne1829\), and both indices are positive. Hence, for the positive parameters \(k=31\) and \(s=1\), the fractional parts are not pairwise distinct.

The conjecture is a universal statement over all positive \(k\) and \(s\), and it asserts both nonintegrality and pairwise distinctness. A failure of the pairwise-distinctness part for even one positive pair \((k,s)\) is enough to refute the whole conjunction. The collision above therefore disproves the conjecture.
